01

ETH ROBOTICS · SEPTEMBER 2026 — PRESENT

Building a
myoelectric prosthetic arm

Starting from scratch, with a focus on research, controls, and machining.

ProstheticsControlsPrototyping

I’m currently prototyping a myoelectric prosthetic arm at ETH. The project brings together my interest in robotics and the hands-on process of developing a physical system from the beginning.

My work focuses on researching the approach, developing controls, and machining parts for the prototype. It is an ongoing build, and I’m interested in how decisions about the mechanism affect the way the system can be controlled.

My focus on this project +
  • Researching approaches for the prosthetic arm prototype.
  • Working on controls and the relationship between motion and mechanical design.
  • Machining and prototyping physical components.

In development

02

TOYON RESEARCH CORPORATION · 2025 — 2026

Automating motor magnet insertion
for motor manufacturing

An automated motor assembly project, developed through months of independent research and iteration.

CADMotor controlRaspberry PiFabrication

During my internship at Toyon Research Corporation, I created a fully automated end-effector for a motor-manufacturing robotic arm. I worked through the research, design, fabrication, integration, and testing needed to turn the initial concept into a working system.

I used CAD to develop the mechanical assembly and integrated motors, drivers, sensors, and control hardware. The design went through repeated rounds of 3D printing and machining until the system operated reliably.

What I took from the build +

Months of independent research, design, iteration, and testing taught me a myriad of skills in CAD, Raspberry Pi programming, motor control, 3D printing, and machining. I learned to understand how the mechanical, electrical, and software pieces interact, and to debug the full system until it works.

03

UCLA · ELEGANT MIND CLUB

A custom drone
with two eyes

Building the hardware for a drone project exploring stereo vision, object recognition, and a virtual reality interface.

SolidWorksRaspberry PiPythonComputer vision

In the Elegant Mind Club at UCLA, I worked on a custom quadcopter with two cameras. The project explored capturing two views of motion and using object recognition and optical flow to investigate depth.

I designed the chassis components in SolidWorks, using 3D-printed supports and a laser-cut acrylic platform. The supports went through several iterations to account for acceleration, deceleration, and the possibility of a sudden drop.

Hardware and software +

The hardware combined RS2205 motors, Arducam cameras, a Raspberry Pi, a LiPo battery, and a Pixhawk flight controller. The software work explored ArduPilot Mission Planner, camera feeds to a VR headset through Unity and C#, and YOLOv5 for object recognition. Testing also involved a Tello drone.

Original project notes ↗
04

UCLA · KOGAR RESEARCH GROUP

A motorized optic rotator

A custom mechanism and electronics for rotating an optic in a condensed matter research lab.

In the Kogar Research Group at UCLA, I built a motorized mount that rotates an optic. I made the mechanism myself and worked on the electronics that connect the motor to the control system.

This work was part of my experience developing a motorized feedback-control system for an ultrafast electron diffraction setup. I programmed a half-wave plate to respond to laser power fluctuations, reducing drift by 4.5%.

I enjoyed working through both sides of the system: making a physical mount that could move the optic, and building and debugging the electronics needed to control that motion.

05

ELECTRONICS · HANDS-ON BUILD

A start-and-stop timer game

A physical timing game built around a breadboard circuit and numeric display.

I built a game where the player starts and stops a timer. The project brought together a physical circuit, a numeric display, and the timing behavior that makes the game work.

The breadboard build let me work directly with the wiring and test the circuit as I put it together. I like projects like this because you can see the result of each change immediately, and there is always something to trace when it does not behave as expected.

06

COMBAT ROBOTICS

Building a combat robot

Hands-on work with motors, wiring, and a compact robotic platform.

I worked on a combat robot, including the hands-on motor and wiring work that goes into bringing the robot together. The build gave me another way to work with the connection between the mechanical layout and the electrical system.

These photos show the robot with its internal components exposed, the assembled chassis, and the motor connections I worked on. The video captures the robot during the build and testing process.

A LITTLE ABOUT ME

I learn by
building.

I’m pursuing my master’s in Electrical Engineering and Information Technology at ETH Zürich, with a focus on robotics and controls. Before that, I studied Physics and Mathematics of Computation at UCLA.

My work has taken me between experimental physics labs, motor manufacturing, and robotics. I enjoy moving between programming, electronics, CAD, and fabrication—and understanding how those pieces come together.

Outside of my projects, I’ve mentored and tutored students in physics and mathematics. I enjoy helping someone work through a difficult problem and find an approach that makes sense to them.
